lessons.title: Serial rules, parallel hardware
lessons.summary: A 4-bit counter. The hardware computes both next values at once; XBlue lets you read, and prove, the cycle one rule at a time.
text: The hardware is parallel. In each clock cycle the counter computes both candidate next values at once, count + 1 and 0, and a multiplexer at the end picks one. Open the SystemVerilog tab: _t4 = _t3 ? (count + 1) : count is tick, and _t6 = _t5 ? 0 : _t4 is clear. Both data paths sit side by side.

XBlue reads it in order. schedule tick ≫ clear says: run tick, then run clear, which sees what tick wrote. A rule is atomic: its guard decides whether all of its writes happen. So the next count is two small steps, one after the other, instead of a priority between parallel paths.

The proof follows the story. Below the module, spec writes the cycle as those two steps, and next_eq_spec proves that the design itself (mkCounter.design.cycle) computes exactly spec, for every input and every count. Lean checks all 64 cases with decide. Facts such as reset_wins then follow from the story in one line each.
The hardware agrees. The lowering to VBlue is proved correct (lower_correct), so these theorems hold for the SystemVerilog too.
interfaces is an implicit rule that drives every method output; it runs first.
try: Swap the schedule to clear ≫ tick. Lean now reports that next_eq_spec is false. Rewrite spec in the new order, and restate reset_wins: what does a reset do now?
Prove that the counter never wraps: when it is full and there is no reset, it stays at 15.

lessons.title: A pipeline FIFO: deq first, then enq
lessons.summary: One rule for deq, one for enq, run in that order. A full FIFO accepts an item in the cycle it delivers one, and the proof says exactly that, on a list.
text: The hardware. A FIFO that can enqueue and dequeue in the same cycle, even when full, has a path from the dequeue side to the enqueue side: dequeuing frees a slot, and enqueuing uses it in the same cycle. Open the SystemVerilog tab: _t6 is count - 1 when the dequeue fires, and the enqueue's condition _t7 reads _t6, not count. In a netlist that is a combinational path you have to find and trust.

In XBlue it is an order. schedule deq ≫ enq says: run deq, then run enq, which sees what deq wrote. Each rule is atomic: its guard decides whether all of its writes happen. So enq asks count != 2 about the count deq left. The method enq_ready is computed at the start of the cycle and says the same thing: count != 2 || deq_ready.

The proof follows the story, on a list. abs reads the registers as a queue of items: count items starting at rp. spec tells the cycle in schedule order on that list: first deq (q1 is the queue without its head), then enq (append x to q1 if it has room). pipeline_correct proves that the design itself (mkPipeFifo2.design.cycle) refines this: for every state that satisfies the invariant, the new queue, enq_ready, deq_valid and deq_data are what the story says, and the invariant (count ≤ 2, and the pointers agree with count) still holds. The data is generic: Lean case-splits only on the control state.

Consequences are short. full_accepts_while_delivering: a full queue that dequeues also accepts, and the new queue is the old one without its head, plus x. empty_has_nothing: an empty queue is not valid. The lowering is proved correct (lower_correct), so all of this holds for the SystemVerilog too.
data[wp] <= … writes one element of a vector register; slot in the proof reads one back.
try: Swap the schedule to enq ≫ deq. Now deq sees what enq stored: an empty FIFO can pass an item through in the same cycle (a bypass FIFO). Change the methods so that deq_valid and deq_data show the incoming item, rewrite spec in the new order, and prove that an empty queue passes an item through.
Prove full_refuses: a full queue that is not dequeued is not ready, and nothing changes.
Prove that the invariant holds after reset: what is Inv of the all-zero registers? (Then find which part of the design guarantees that reset restores them.)

lessons.title: A round-robin arbiter: fairness you can prove
lessons.summary: Rotate, pick the first, rotate back. The story is a simple scan; the theorems say the grant is one-hot, requested, and fair.
text: The hardware. Open the SystemVerilog tab. A round-robin arbiter is a barrel shifter ({req, req} >> start), a priority mux over four bits, and an adder to rotate the answer back. It is one block of combinational logic. Why is the result fair? You cannot see it in the wires.

XBlue lets you say it as a scan. Most of the module is named values, and the state is one register, last. The cycle has three steps in the schedule: interfaces shows the grant computed from last, advance stores the winner, clear runs last. The rotate trick is only how the hardware finds pick: the first requester when you walk round from last + 1.

The proof checks that the trick is the story. spec uses pick, a plain scan, and next_eq_spec proves that the design (mkArbiter.design.cycle, the grant wire and the next last) computes exactly that, for every request pattern and every last. Lean checks all 128 cases with decide.

Fairness is then easy to state. grant_is_one_hot, grant_is_requested and grant_iff_request are safety. last_winner_yields is the fairness rule: the last winner does not win again while anyone else asks. rotates says that with all four requesting the winner goes 0, 1, 2, 3, 0. Each one rewrites with the story and lets Lean check the cases. The lowering is proved correct (lower_correct), so these hold for the SystemVerilog too.
priority case takes the first arm whose condition holds; unique case would OR the arms (one-hot). Shifts may take a narrower amount, which is zero-extended.
try: Set req to 0xf (all request) in the stimulus: the winner should rotate 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, … Which theorem says so?
Prove sole_requester: if only requester 2 asks (req = 4), it wins whatever last is.
Make it a fixed-priority arbiter by replacing start with 0. next_eq_spec now fails. Change pick to match, and replace the fairness theorems by one that is true.

lessons.title: GCD: each rule keeps the answer
lessons.summary: Euclid by subtraction. Each rule keeps gcd x y, so the invariant is proved one rule at a time.
text: The hardware is a chain. Open the SystemVerilog tab. Because the schedule chains the rules with ≫, the emitted wires are a chain too: _t5 is finish, _t7 to _t9 are load, _t11 and _t12 are swap, _t14 is subtract, _t16 is clear. Each stage reads the one before it. One cycle can load, swap and subtract.

Each rule is one step of Euclid's algorithm, guarded by when the step is legal: swap when x < y, subtract when x ≥ y. A rule is atomic: its guard decides whether all of its writes happen. So the cycle is five small steps in a fixed order, and the proof can take them one at a time.

The proof follows the story. Below the module, each rule is written as a plain function on the registers (finish, load, swap, subtract, clear), and spec composes them in schedule order. next_eq_spec proves that the design itself (mkGcd.design.cycle) equals that composition, for every input and state. This is a 40-bit statement, so Lean hands it to bv_decide, a SAT solver, rather than enumerating cases.

The invariant is proved rule by rule. swap_keeps_gcd is gcd x y = gcd y x. subtract_keeps_gcd is gcd (x - y) y = gcd x y. They are two small lemmas about two small functions. busy_cycle_keeps_gcd then follows for the whole cycle by rewriting through the story. load_starts_gcd says a load starts a computation of gcd a b, and done_is_gcd says that when y = 0 the register x is the gcd. Together: the result is the gcd. The lowering is proved correct (lower_correct), so this holds for the SystemVerilog too.
The stimulus loads gcd(48, 18) at cycle 1 and gcd(105, 30) at cycle 20; watch io_done and io_result.
try: Move subtract before swap in the schedule. next_eq_spec fails. Fix spec to the new order: does any lemma about the gcd need to change?
Prove finish_clears: when busy is set, y = 0, and there is no reset and no new start, one cycle leaves x and y alone and clears busy.
Try swap ∥ subtract: both write x, so it is rejected. What would the story look like if it were allowed?

lessons.title: A pipelined multiplier: what the registers mean
lessons.summary: Two stages, latest stage first. The story shows each stage reading its predecessor's old value, and the proof says the product appears two cycles later.
text: The hardware. Open the SystemVerilog tab. _t5 computes the next p from lo and hi, and _t8 and _t9 compute the next lo and hi from the inputs. All three are plain flip-flop inputs, in parallel. Nothing in the wires says that p is a product, or when.

The order of the rules is the pipeline. A register written by one rule is visible to the rules after it in the same cycle. schedule stage2 ≫ stage1 puts the later stage first, so stage2 reads the old lo and hi before stage1 overwrites them. Each register is a pipeline boundary. You can read this off the schedule; you do not have to find it in the netlist.

The proof follows the story. spec tells the cycle in that order: first stage2 (it uses the registers as they were at the start of the cycle), then stage1, then clear. next_eq_spec proves that the design itself (mkMul2.design.cycle) equals the story, for every input and every state. The proof is one simp.

What the pipeline computes. product_after_two_cycles runs the design for two cycles from any state, with any inputs in the second cycle, and says that p is in_a × in_b of the first. It follows from the story in a few lines: the low and high partial products add up to the whole product (a fact about b's nibbles that Lean checks over all 256 values). valid_after_two_cycles says the valid bit travels with it. Because the start state is arbitrary, this holds at every cycle. The lowering is proved correct (lower_correct), so it holds for the SystemVerilog too.
Gates shows the cost: two 16×16 multipliers before optimisation, narrowed by wreduce.
try: Swap to stage1 ≫ stage2. next_eq_spec now fails. Change spec so that stage2 reads what stage1 wrote, and state the new product theorem: how many cycles does it take?
Prove p_ignores_inputs: the new value of p does not depend on this cycle's inputs, only on the old lo and hi. This is what a pipeline register means.
Compute the whole product in one rule (p <= a16 * zeroExtend(in_b);), and rewrite the story and the theorem to match. Compare depth in Gates.

lessons.title: Cache-line state: the story finds the bug
lessons.summary: Valid / dirty bits for four lines, one operation per request. Reading the cycle in schedule order shows why the writeback counter never moves.
text: The hardware. Open the SystemVerilog tab. Each op rule has a chain of wires for valid and dirty: _t6 is the read miss, _t9 and _t10 the write, _t12 and _t13 the evict. The counter's enable _t14 is built from _t12 and _t13, not from the registers. That is easy to miss in a page of wires.

XBlue reads it in order. Each line moves Invalid → Clean (read miss) → Dirty (write) → Invalid (evict). The guards select exactly one op rule per request. Because valid is written by three rules they are chained with ≫, and every rule sees what the rules before it wrote. In spec that is a list of lets: valid1 after readMiss, valid2 after write, valid3 after evict. countWb is the next line, and it reads valid3 and dirty3.

The proof checks the story and the story shows the bug. next_eq_spec proves that the design itself (mkLineState.design.cycle) equals spec, for every request and every state. The state is wide, so Lean hands it to bv_decide. Then writebacks_stuck falls out: countWb asks whether the line is valid and dirty after evict has cleared both, so its guard is never true and writebacks never changes. The simulation pane shows the same thing as a blocked rule (amber). The proof says it for all inputs.

An invariant, one rule at a time. inv_preserved: a line is dirty only if it is valid. readMiss only sets valid, write sets both, evict clears both, clear clears both, so the invariant survives each step. evict_invalidates says an evict leaves the line invalid. The lowering is proved correct (lower_correct), so these hold for the SystemVerilog too.
try: Fix the writeback counter: move countWb before evict in the schedule. Change spec the same way, and replace writebacks_stuck by a theorem that says a dirty eviction is counted.
Prove read_miss_counted: a read of an invalid line adds one to misses.
Add a flush op (req_op == 3) that clears every dirty bit. Extend spec with the new rule, and prove that a flush leaves no line dirty. Does the invariant still hold?

lessons.title: Schedules decide throughput
lessons.summary: A 2-stage pipeline whose rate depends only on the order of ≫. The story makes the difference a short proof.
text: The hardware. Open the SystemVerilog tab. The three rules are a chain: _t4 is v2 after drain, _t5 (the exec guard) reads _t4 and not v2, and _t9 (the fetch guard) reads _t8, the v1 that exec left. Reversing the schedule rewires the chain; no rule changes.

XBlue reads it in order. With drain ≫ exec ≫ fetch, each rule sees the slot its successor freed in this cycle: exec sees a free stage 2 because drain just emptied it, and fetch sees a free stage 1 because exec just emptied it. In spec that is three let blocks in schedule order, and step_eq_spec proves that the design itself (mkPipe2.design.cycle) equals them for every state.

Throughput is then a short proof. full_speed: with both stages full and a ready consumer, every stage moves at once and the pipeline is full again. fetches_every_cycle: whenever the consumer is ready, a new item is fetched, so there are no bubbles. stalls: with both stages full and the consumer not ready, no guard holds and nothing changes, so the guards alone give back-pressure. The lowering is proved correct (lower_correct), so these hold for the SystemVerilog too.

The consumer sees out_valid and out_data as they were at the start of the cycle (the interfaces rule runs first). Try the stall in the Simulation pane: out_ready is low for four cycles and the pipeline fills.
try: Change the schedule to fetch ≫ exec ≫ drain ≫ clear. All three theorems stop being true. Write the new spec, and prove what the consumer sees: consumer_sees_nothing.
Prove latency_two: an item fetched into an empty pipeline is in stage 2 two cycles later, whatever the consumer does.
Try (exec ∥ fetch): both write v1, so the front end rejects it.

lessons.title: Exercise: fix the credit counter
lessons.summary: Two bugs: the compiler finds the first, and a failing proof of the invariant finds the second.
text: A sender has 4 credits. take spends one per request, give returns one per response; io_ok checks credits + inflight == 4. That is the invariant: every credit is either in the sender or out with a request.

The compiler finds the first bug. It does not compile. The error is on the schedule line: what do take and give both write? Rules in parallel read the same start state, so one of the two updates to credits would be lost. The front end refuses.

A proof finds the second. Simulation can show that io_ok drops, but only if your stimulus gets there. With the story you can ask the question for every state. Write a spec that tells the cycle one rule at a time, and try to prove that the invariant is preserved. Where the proof fails, there is a state where it is false: read the guard of take in that state.

The first answer fixes the schedule and shows the failure as a theorem (second_bug). The second fixes the guard and proves inv_preserved. The lowering is proved correct (lower_correct), so the invariant holds for the SystemVerilog too.
try: Hint 1: take ≫ give lets both fire in one cycle, and give sees take's new sent. In the story, what is inflight at the point where give's guard is evaluated?
Hint 2: with 4 in flight, credits is 0. Should take fire? Try to prove inv_preserved with the current guard, and look at the state where it fails.

lessons.title: A router's matrix arbiter: fairness as a theorem
lessons.summary: From the CcNoc router: a priority matrix that gives the last winner the lowest priority. The story makes the fairness argument a short proof.
text: The hardware. Each output port of the CcNoc router (XBlue/Examples/CcNoc/Router.lean) has an arbiter like this one, cut here to 3 requesters. Open the SystemVerilog tab: the grant is one expression over nine bits of pb and three request bits, and the new matrix is nine more muxes, _t3, that all depend on the winner. Why is it fair? The wires do not say.

The story is short. Bit 3*i+j of pb says requester i is above j, and a requester wins when it asks and no asking requester is above it. permit and winner are functions over an Integer index: the front end unrolls them, so the hardware is plain gates. In the story they are above, wins and winner. The cycle is then two steps in schedule order: update moves the winner to the bottom (its row is cleared, its column set), and clear runs last. next_eq_spec proves that the design itself (mkMatrixArbiter3.design.cycle) equals that story for every request and every matrix.

Fairness is then one theorem. winner_waits: after update, every other asking requester is above the winner, so the winner is blocked. no_repeat says it at the level of a clock cycle: a requester that just won cannot win the next cycle while another one asks. grants_rotate checks the example: all three asking from reset gives 1, 2, 4. grant_is_one_hot says at most one grant is raised. The lowering is proved correct (lower_correct), so these hold for the SystemVerilog too.
pb[k : k] <= v writes one bit; the writes of one rule are put back together into one register write.
try: Hold all three requests high (req = 7) and watch io_grant rotate 1, 2, 4. Which theorem says so?
Swap the schedule to clear ≫ update. next_eq_spec fails. Rewrite spec in the new order, and prove that a reset with requests no longer leaves the matrix at 0x0ee.
Prove lone_requester: if only requester 2 asks and the diagonal bit pb[8] is clear, it wins. Why does the proof need the diagonal?

lessons.title: A blocking cache: blocked means blocked
lessons.summary: The shape of the CcNoc L2 slice: hits from the arrays, a miss walks a small state machine. The proof says nothing else gets in until it is done.
text: The hardware. The CcNoc system's caches (stage 1, ported from Bluespec) are blocking: while a miss is being served, req_ready is low and nothing else gets in. This one has 4 lines of 8 bits. In the SystemVerilog the control state is one 2-bit register, and four independent-looking enables read it. Whether "nothing else gets in" is true depends on which copy of state each enable reads.

XBlue reads it in order. RegFiles are arrays: a read sees the start of the cycle, and an upd lands at the clock edge, as in a Bluespec register. The miss states are rules with exclusive guards on state, and the schedule runs them backwards, fill ≫ writeBack ≫ access, so each state lasts one cycle. A rule sees what earlier rules wrote, so access must not look at state where it runs: fill may just have set it to Ready. It uses req_ready, which interfaces computed from the state at the start of the cycle (the Bluespec original also tests a start-of-cycle copy).

The proof follows the story. spec tells the control registers' cycle in that order: fill, writeBack, access, clear. step_eq_spec proves that the design itself (mkBlockingCache.design.cycle) equals it, for every state, request and tag array (the array read is one opaque value, and bv_decide does the rest).

Then "blocking" is a theorem. blocked_ignores_requests: if the state is not Ready, the next registers do not depend on the request inputs at all. writeback_then_fill: WriteBack lasts one cycle, Fill waits for mem_rvalid and then returns to Ready. miss_latches: a miss records the request and leaves Ready. state_ok: the state is never 3. The lowering is proved correct (lower_correct), so these hold for the SystemVerilog too.
try: Make access read state == 0 directly instead of req_ready. Which theorem stops being true? Replace it by one that shows the cache taking a request while req_ready is low.
Reverse the schedule to access ≫ writeBack ≫ fill ≫ clear. Rewrite spec in the new order and prove what a miss does when memory answers at once.
Prove hit_keeps_control: a hit in Ready changes no control register.

lessons.title: MSHRs: every new miss has a request
lessons.summary: Two miss registers: hit-under-miss, miss-under-miss, secondary misses merged. The proof ties each MSHR to a memory request.
text: The hardware. Stage 2 of the CcNoc tutorial replaces the blocking L1 with a non-blocking one (L1NB.lean). Its heart is a small file of MSHRs: a miss takes a free one and asks memory; a load to a line that already has an MSHR waits on it (a secondary miss, merged: no second request); a hit is answered at once, even with misses outstanding. In the SystemVerilog the methods ld_ready and mem_req are computed from mshr at the start of the cycle (_t1, _t4), and the update is a separate chain of muxes. Do the two agree?

XBlue reads it in order. Reg#(Vector#(2, Mshr)) mshr is one register holding two structs; mshr[i] <= … writes one element and e with { f = v } updates one field. A rule sees what the rules before it wrote, so the order matters. schedule load ≫ fill runs load on the MSHRs as the methods saw them, then fill frees the one memory answered. load either merges into the MSHR for its line or takes a free one.

The proof follows the story. spec tells the cycle in that order: load, fill, clear, with the outputs mem_req and ld_ready read from the start. step_eq_spec proves that the design itself (mkTwoMSHRs.design.cycle) equals it, for every state, input and present array (the array read is one opaque bit, and bv_decide does the rest).

Then the key facts are theorems. no_duplicates: at most one MSHR per line, in every cycle. secondary_no_request: a line that already has an MSHR makes no memory request. new_mshr_has_request: whenever an entry becomes valid for a new line, mem_req was raised, so no MSHR waits for a request that was never made. The lowering is proved correct (lower_correct), so these hold for the SystemVerilog too.
Answers are not ordered: resp_tag says which load a response belongs to.
try: Prove second_load_merges: two loads to the same line from an empty file. The first asks memory, the second merges. Use the stimulus ld_line = 3 and no fills to watch it.
Prove busy_not_ready: with both MSHRs busy on other lines, a load that misses is not ready. Use fill_valid always 0 to watch it.

Swap the schedule to fill ≫ load ≫ clear. step_eq_spec fails (it needs the new order), and so does new_mshr_has_request. Rewrite spec, and replace that theorem by one that shows an MSHR reused without a request.
